record.paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
record.original_question: What are the present compositions and internal structures of Uranus and Neptune: how are hydrogen-helium, water, rock or refractory material, methane, ammonia, and other heavy elements distributed with depth; are the interiors best described by distinct layers or by continuous composition gradients; and which density profiles can fit the planets' measured mass, radius, rotation, and gravity data?

evidence.quote: Key fundamental questions regarding Uranus and Neptune remain open, such as: Key questions regarding Uranus and Neptune include: +What are the compositions and internal structures of Uranus and Neptune?
However, accurate measurements are insufficient to uniquely infer the planetary structure and composition, given the degenerate nature of the problem.
As a result, the compositions and internal structures of these planets are poorly determined.
It is important to note that such structure models with distinct layers of different compositions are likely unrealistic since rock and water can be mixed as well as water and hydrogen.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Model a giant planet as a self-gravitating, rotating fluid body in hydrostatic equilibrium, characterized by a spherically- or oblately-symmetric mass density profile ρ(r) (possibly with latitudinal dependence due to rotation) and a depth-dependent composition specifying the local mass fractions of hydrogen–helium, water, rock/refractory material, methane, ammonia, and other heavy elements. Given the following observational constraints for Uranus and (separately) Neptune:

  • total mass M,
  • mean radius R at the 1 bar pressure level,
  • rotation period (and hence angular velocity Ω),
  • the measured low-order even gravitational harmonics J₂ and J₄ (defined by the external gravitational potential expansion U(r,θ) = (GM/r)[1 − Σ_{n≥1} J_{2n}(R/r)^{2n} P_{2n}(cosθ)]),

and using a thermodynamically consistent equation of state P(ρ,T,X) for mixtures of the species above with a prescribed thermal profile (e.g.\ adiabatic in convective regions), determine:

(a) the radial distribution of each chemical component, i.e. the functions X_i(r) for i ∈ {H/He, H₂O, rock, CH₄, NH₃, other heavies};

(b) whether the interior is best represented by a small number of chemically distinct layers separated by sharp boundaries, or by smoothly varying composition gradients (and in the latter case, identify the gradient profiles);

(c) the full set, or a representative family, of density profiles ρ(r) (and associated composition profiles) that simultaneously reproduce the observed M, R, Ω, J₂, and J₄ to within their measurement uncertainties.

Describe and, where possible, quantify the non-uniqueness (degeneracy) of solutions consistent with these constraints.
artifact.status_search_result: The composition and internal structure of Uranus and Neptune remain open problems in planetary science. Available gravity, mass, radius, and rotation data are insufficient to uniquely determine interior density and composition profiles; recent modeling work continues to produce multiple, observationally indistinguishable layered and gradient-based structure models, and resolving the degeneracy is a stated motivation for future ice-giant missions.
